title: ⭐⭐ Revision: naming the giver, joining the text

questions.prompt: Match each phrasal verb with the meaning it carries.

options.text: gain the favour and the support of people
meet people you have not seen for a while

questions.explanation: catch up with old friends means to meet people you have not seen for a while: the phrasal verb is about the gap of time you close, not about speed. come round to somebody's house means to pay somebody an informal visit; the particle round carries the short trip, and nothing is handed over. take over a family business means to assume responsibility for something, so the person who takes over becomes the one in charge. win a committee over means to gain the favour and the support of people, and it is the only one of the four that can split around its object: win them over, never win over them.

questions.prompt: Some of these words name a person; the others name an act or a quality. Which ones name a person?
questions.explanation: altruist carries -ist, the suffix English hangs on a noun in -ism to name the person who lives by it. donor is built on donate with -or, the small closed group of verbs that take that ending instead of -er. fund-raiser is built on the verb phrase raise funds with -er, the ordinary agent ending. The three others name something else: altruism is the quality itself, the unselfish concern for other people; donation is one act of giving, not the giver; and endowment is the permanent fund, while the person who provides it is an endower.

questions.prompt: A report praises the association for being a "well-run philanthropy". What does the phrase say about it?

options.text: It has been running for a long time.
It organises races to collect money.
It spends more than it receives.

questions.explanation: well-run is an adverb followed by a past participle, so somebody runs it well and run here means manage: "It is managed efficiently." "It has been running for a long time." reads run as duration, but the adverb well says how the thing is done, never how long. "It organises races to collect money." takes run in its athletic sense, which the compound does not carry. "It spends more than it receives." describes a badly run organisation, the very opposite of the praise.

questions.prompt: A volunteer answers a journalist with two words: "Since 2016." Which question was she asked?

options.text: When did the association open its second centre?
How long did the association run the second centre?
How many people has the association helped this year?
How long has the association run the second centre?

questions.explanation: Since plus a year gives the point where a period begins and says that the period is still open, so only a question in the present perfect asking how long fits: "How long has the association run the second centre?" "When did the association open its second centre?" asks for a finished moment and is answered by In 2016, not by Since 2016. "How long did the association run the second centre?" shuts the period inside the past, so its answer would be For four years and the centre would have closed. "How many people has the association helped this year?" asks for a number, not for a starting point.

questions.prompt: A pupil writing a report has just given her first argument. She now wants to add a second one that she considers stronger than the first. Which marker opens it?
questions.explanation: "Besides," is the marker that announces an argument the writer considers stronger than the one before it, which is precisely what she wants. "Similarly," presents an argument of the same weight pointing the same way, so it flattens the difference she is trying to make. "To begin with," opens a list and cannot come once the first argument has already been given. "Earlier," places something in time, before another event, and says nothing at all about the strength of an argument.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The waiting list gets longer every month. It's high time the town ___ a public library."
questions.explanation: After it's high time English uses a past form although the sentence is about now and about something overdue, so the town "built" a public library. "builds" puts the present where that expression never allows one. "will build" pushes the library into the future, and the whole point of it's high time is that the moment has already arrived. "has built" would say the library is finished, which contradicts a waiting list that is still growing.
